query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially replacing Hf with additional Zr in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower the overall density without significantly sacrificing the solid solution strengthening and mechanical performance at room temperature and up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr alloy having a density of around 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by substituting a portion of Hf with additional Zr so that the new alloy contains relatively more Zr at the expense of Hf.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under standard tensile or compression loading at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to ~1000 °C, with processing conditions similar to the as-cast state.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase solid-solution (likely BCC) structure with similar lattice distortions that provide solid solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: Since Hf is one of the heavier elements in the alloy, its partial replacement with lighter Zr (which has a comparable atomic size) can reduce the alloy density. Moreover, because Zr has been shown to maintain elevated-temperature strength when incorporated into similar alloy systems, the lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening are expected to be largely preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in alloy density compared to the original as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, while the yield strength and ductility at both room temperature and approximately 1000 °C remain comparable.
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and demonstrated high strength in current mechanical testing regimes.
generation.boundary: The proposed benefits should be observable under service conditions that range from room temperature to ~1000 °C and under standard loading conditions used in comparing tensile/compressive properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage of density reduction and the precise limits for retained mechanical properties depend on the level of Hf substitution by Zr; additional experiments are needed to optimize the composition and verify phase stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of modified alloys where a controlled fraction of Hf is replaced by Zr (e.g., 10%, 20%, and 30% substitution levels). Process the alloys via casting to achieve homogeneous microstructures. Measure density using the Archimedes method and perform tensile and compressive tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C. Confirm phase stability through X-ray diffraction to ensure a continuous single-phase solid solution.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and elongation/dactility at room temperature and ~1000 °C
XRD for phase composition and homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloys do not show a significant density reduction compared with the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if there is a substantial drop in mechanical performance (e.g., yield strength or ductility decreases by more than about 10-15%) or phase segregation is observed, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System

Abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys (HEA) are promising materials for high temperature applications. This work presents investigations of the room temperature tensile mechanical properties of selected 3 and 4 elements medium entropy alloys (MEA) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system. Tensile testing was combined with fractographic and microstructure analysis, using scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength dispersive spectroscope (WDS) and X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD). The 5 element HEA alloy HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation while 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength. Some of them are ductile, some of them brittle, depending on microstructure. Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content. Precipitation of Ta rich particles on grain boundaries reduces further the maximum elongation to failure down to zero values.

Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility).
